original_summary: The Ultimatum Game: a Proposer offers a Responder part of 100 units. If the Responder accepts, the split stands; if the Responder rejects, both get 0. It is one-shot, with complete information about the pot.

review.evidence: In the one-shot original the offer-minimum/accept-anything pair is the subgame-perfect answer. Under 'higher total wins' with two players, only the difference counts, so the Responder rejects anything under 50 and the game collapses to a forced 50/50 draw. The previous 3-player variation still degenerated. Always taking the first option (offer 0, accept) won 60 of 60 games as seat 1 and as seat 2. Always taking the last option lost 60 of 60. Seat 3 won only 7 times against random seats, a structural seat bias.

A fixed one-line policy beat random players every time. Rejection was cheap for everyone except the proposer's rivals, and nothing hidden needed reading, so skill had little to work on beyond 'be stingy'.
With the pot public, the only question is how fairness norms hold up. Once the answer is known (lowball in the original, 50/50 under relative scoring), nothing is left to improve.
Complete information: the Responder knows exactly what the Proposer keeps. There is no hidden state, no type to infer, and in the one-shot form no multi-round plan.
Payoffs follow by arithmetic from the offer and the accept or reject decision.
The game is turn-based, text-only, short and numeric: a sequential choice followed by a response.

problems: Offering the minimum and always accepting is near-dominant. In the previous variation the 'first option' policy won 100% of games against random seats.
Rejection is not a credible threat: a stingy offer costs the Proposer nothing extra when it fails, and against non-punishing responders it pays the most.
Rejection must not become free either. If only the Proposer pays for a failed deal, 'always reject' quietly drags rivals down and becomes a thoughtless winning policy.
The pot is public, so there is nothing to infer. The Responder can compute the Proposer's keep exactly.
Seat imbalance: a 1-2-3 proposer rotation, with the lower seat always first Responder, left seat 3 winning far less often even against random play.
With two players and 'higher total wins', only the difference matters, so the game is a forced 50/50 draw. The one-shot form has no repeated-play reasoning at all.
A random pot size per round would be a lottery: whoever is dealt bigger pots as Proposer gets ahead for no reason.

changes.what: Three players. The Proposer seat rotates in snake order 1,2,3,3,2,1 over 6 rounds, so each player proposes exactly twice. The two Responders choose at the same moment, so neither is 'first'.
changes.why: Three players break the zero-sum difference trap. The snake order gives every seat one early and one late proposal. Simultaneous responses remove the lower-seat ordering.
changes.fixes: Seat imbalance: a 1-2-3 proposer rotation, with the lower seat always first Responder, left seat 3 winning far less often even against random play.

changes.what: The deal passes only if BOTH Responders accept. If it fails, the Proposer loses one third (rounded down) of the amount they tried to keep.
changes.why: A stingy offer that gets vetoed now costs the Proposer heavily. A generous offer risks little, but hands rivals points. Both ends of the offer range are risky. Against purely random responders (25% pass), the penalty makes the expected value of proposing about zero for any keep, so lowballing no longer beats random play.
changes.fixes: Offering the minimum and always accepting is near-dominant. In the previous variation the 'first option' policy won 100% of games against random seats.

changes.what: Every Responder who rejects pays 1 point.
changes.why: A veto must be worth its cost. Always-reject now loses about 4 points over the game and never earns as a Responder, so it falls behind.
changes.fixes: Rejection must not become free either. If only the Proposer pays for a failed deal, 'always reject' quietly drags rivals down and becomes a thoughtless winning policy.

changes.what: The pot is hidden. Each player proposes once with a pot of 12 and once with a pot of 24, in a secret random order. Only the Proposer knows the current pot. Offers are capped at 0–6 per Responder. Pots, keeps and running totals stay private until the game ends; only offers, votes and pass or fail are public.
changes.why: Responders must infer from an offer (and any talk) whether the Proposer is splitting fairly or lowballing a big pot. Proposers with a big pot want to look like they have a small one. Because every player gets the same two pots, the draw changes what players know, not who is ahead.
changes.fixes: The pot is public, so there is nothing to infer. The Responder can compute the Proposer's keep exactly.

changes.what: Every player gets the same pair of pots (12 and 24); only the order is random.
changes.why: The random draw affects only information and timing, not total opportunity, so it is not a lottery.
changes.fixes: A random pot size per round would be a lottery: whoever is dealt bigger pots as Proposer gets ahead for no reason.

changes.what: Six rounds, the highest final total wins outright, and a tie for highest is a draw. A simultaneous one-message talk phase is held before each offer.
changes.why: Repetition lets players build a reputation and retaliate. Talk lets Proposers claim a pot size (truthfully or not) and lets Responders threaten vetoes. Interests conflict because only one player can win.
changes.fixes: With two players and 'higher total wins', only the difference matters, so the game is a forced 50/50 draw. The one-shot form has no repeated-play reasoning at all.

keeps: A Proposer divides a pot and the Responders can only accept or reject. Rejection destroys the round's value for everyone.
The core tension between keeping more and offering enough to avoid rejection.
Simple integer offers and arithmetic payoffs.

recommendation.reason: The ultimatum tension is worth training on once rejection is costly on both sides, the pot is private and the seats are balanced. All of this fits within a dozen steps per round.

variation.name: Hidden-Pot Ultimatum (Three Players)
variation.summary: Three players take turns as Proposer, twice each. The Proposer secretly knows whether the pot is 12 or 24 and offers each of the two Responders 0–6 points. Both Responders must accept or the deal fails. A failed deal costs the Proposer a third of their intended keep and costs each rejecter 1 point. The highest total after 6 rounds wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP: Three players, seats 1, 2 and 3. Everyone starts with 0 points. Totals are private: each player is told only their own total until the game ends. Each player will propose in exactly two rounds. For each player, one of those two rounds has a pot of 12 and the other a pot of 24. The order is secret and random.

PROPOSER ORDER: Round 1: seat 1. Round 2: seat 2. Round 3: seat 3. Round 4: seat 3. Round 5: seat 2. Round 6: seat 1. In each round the other two players are the Responders.

EACH ROUND:
1. Announce the round number and who the Proposer is.
2. Pot. If this is the Proposer's first proposal, the engine flips a fair coin: heads means the pot is 12 this time (and 24 next time), tails means 24 this time (and 12 next time). If it is the Proposer's second proposal, the pot is whichever value was not used the first time.
3. Tell the pot privately to the Proposer only.
4. Talk: all three players each write one short message at the same time, without seeing the others' messages. The Proposer may state, hint at or lie about the pot. Nothing said is binding.
5. Show all three messages to everyone.
6. The Proposer chooses two whole numbers: an offer to each Responder, each from 0 to 6. The two offers may differ. The Proposer's keep is the pot minus both offers (always at least 0).
7. Announce both offers to everyone. The pot and the keep are not announced.
8. The two Responders each choose Accept or Reject at the same time.
9. Announce both votes.
10. If both accepted, the deal passes: each Responder adds their offer to their total, and the Proposer adds their keep.
11. If at least one rejected, the deal fails: nobody receives an offer or a keep. The Proposer instead loses one third of their keep, rounded down (keep 12 loses 4, keep 6 loses 2, keep 2 loses 0).
12. In either case, each Responder who chose Reject loses 1 point.
13. Tell each player privately their own new total.

END: After round 6, reveal every round's pot and keep and every player's total. Totals may be negative.
variation.objective: The player with the strictly highest final total wins. If two or three players tie for the highest total, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect:
Lowballing (offers 0/0) now loses heavily whenever either Responder vetoes. With a 24 pot that is 8 points per veto, so first-option play no longer beats random seats. A rough expectation against random players puts it behind them. Maximum generosity (6/6) hands rivals 12 points, and always-reject bleeds about 4 points, so last-option play loses too.

Good play means calibrating offers to the hidden pot and judging whether an offer of, say, 4/4 is a fair 12-pot split or a 24-pot grab. Uneven offers can buy one Responder while testing the other's willingness to veto at a cost of 1. A Proposer can manage their reputation across their two turns: the second pot is known to them but not to the others.

Talk earns its place. Proposers can bluff about the pot. Responders can threaten or promise vetoes. The players disagree because only one can win. A Responder who simply follows the Proposer's 'it's a small pot, accept 4' may be handing a rival a 16-point keep. A Proposer who believes a veto threat may give away more than needed.

The snake order and the identical pot pairs remove seat and draw advantages.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFFS PER ROUND. Pot P is 12 or 24. Offers are a and b, each from 0 to 6. Keep k = P - a - b, which is always at least 0 because a + b <= 12 <= P.
- Deal passes: Proposer +k, Responder A +a, Responder B +b.
- Deal fails: Proposer -floor(k/3), and each rejecter -1.

SWING CAUSED BY ONE REJECTION (offer 6,6):
| Pot | Keep | Proposer swing | Rejecter swing | Other Responder swing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 0 | 0 | -7 | -6 |
| 24 | 12 | -16 | -7 | -6 |

SWING CAUSED BY ONE REJECTION (offer 0,0):
| Pot | Keep | Proposer swing | Rejecter swing | Other Responder swing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 12 | -16 | -1 | 0 |
| 24 | 24 | -32 | -1 | 0 |

Rejection is a cheap punishment of greedy proposers in a winner-take-all game. Accepting is better in raw points but not in relative standing, so neither vote is dominant. Neither is any offer: high offers cost keep, low offers invite rejection.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, by the winner rule:
(a) Always offer 0,0 and always accept.
- Against copies of itself: everyone ends on 36, a draw.
- Against punishing responders who reject low offers: it loses 16 in its pot-12 round and 32 in its pot-24 round, ending near -16 while others are near 0 or above. It LOSES.
(b) Always offer 6,6 and always accept.
- Against greedy opponents who offer it 0 but accept: it ends on 12 (keep 0 + 12), each opponent on 48 (36 + 12). It LOSES.
(c) Always reject.
- It takes -1 in each of 4 responder rounds, so -4.
- Rational opponents reject its proposals, costing it about floor(k/3), up to 4 + 8 = 12, so it ends near -16. Opponents lose at most 4 each from their pot-24 rounds. It LOSES.
(d) Random play: random votes sink about 75% of deals. Both greedy and generous fixed policies are beaten by players who tailor offers and votes.
No policy wins or draws against every opponent.

SEAT ORDER. Proposer order is 1,2,3,3,2,1. The retaliation window is the maximum offers that can later be withheld from that proposer:
| Seat | Proposals | Later proposals that can punish | Max withheld |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | R1, R6 | R1: R2-R5 (24); R6: none (0) | 24 |
| 2 | R2, R5 | R2: R3, R4, R6 (18); R5: R6 (6) | 24 |
| 3 | R3, R4 | R3: R5, R6 (12); R4: R5, R6 (12) | 24 |
Each seat proposes twice, once with 12 and once with 24. Every second proposal is equally inferable from the first. No seat has a structural edge, and all three can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
Rules are complete:
- Offer ranges 0-6 guarantee keep >= 0.
- The fail case is fully specified, including rounding (keep 0 loses 0) and both responders rejecting (each -1).
- The second pot is deterministic.
- The winner is the strict highest total, otherwise a draw.

The game is finite at 6 rounds and decided by arithmetic on kept totals.

Limits:
| Item | Used | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| steps_per_round | 13 | 20 |
| choice_steps_per_round (talk, offer pair, votes) | 3 | 4 |
| attributes | 13 | 20 |
| hidden_elements (pots, private totals) | 2 | 3 |
| random_draws_per_round (coin only on first proposal) | 1 | 1 |
| rounds | 6 | 40 |

Engine support: hidden pot and private totals map to private_values, offers to numeric_bids, votes to simultaneous_choice, and talk to free_text_talk.

Talk is simultaneous and placed where players genuinely conflict. The proposer wants to hide or understate the pot, and responders want to coordinate rejection threats or plead. Following a claim can cost them. No board, clock, judge, trading or binding agreement is needed.

Late rounds: rejection stays a live, cheap punishment in every round including R6, so 'always accept' does not win the late rounds.
